prompt.context: Our client is a large grocery store chain owner in France. The chain operates 150 stores across France, through two types of facilities: large grocery stores and small convenience stores. The client's annual revenues are €45B a year, 85% of which is through large grocery stores. Our client, Jean-Paul LeTrouc, has indicated that recently sales have been declining. Jean-Paul believes that online grocery sales may be one cause for the decline in sales, and has asked McKinsey to look into it.
prompt.question: What are some key areas for Jean-Paul to consider when thinking about an entry into the online grocery market?

clarifying_info.q: Do we have any information on the size of the French grocery market, both through traditional channels and online?
clarifying_info.a: Present the candidate with the online grocery penetration exhibit showing data for UK (60M pop, €6,000M online sales, 4% penetration), Spain (50M pop, €750M online sales, 1% penetration), Sweden (9M pop, €175M online sales, 1% penetration), and France (65M pop, unknown sales, unknown penetration).

clarifying_info.q: Where will France's per capita online grocery consumption land?
clarifying_info.a: It will be less than the UK but more than Spain and Sweden. The candidate should estimate based on their knowledge of the countries.

clarifying_info.q: What share of the online market will our client capture, and how much is cannibalization vs new sales?
clarifying_info.a: Assume our client captures the entire online market, and that 70% of online sales are cannibalized from existing retail stores while 30% are new sales.

exhibits.title: Online Grocery Penetration Rate for Select Countries
exhibits.shows: A table comparing online grocery market data across four countries: UK, Spain, Sweden, and France. For each country it shows population (millions), online grocery sales per year (millions of euros), and penetration rate (% of groceries bought online). France's online sales and penetration rate are unknown.

exhibits.title: Retail vs Online Basket Economics
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of average basket size, contribution breakdown, and operating income for the retail store channel versus the online channel. Contribution is approximately 25% of the average basket size for both channels.

framework: External: Size of French grocery market
External: Size of online grocery market
Internal: Incremental revenues from online entry
Internal: Incremental costs of online channel

questions.prompt: Estimate the size of the online grocery market in France.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate per capita online grocery consumption for benchmark countries, note the UK is an outlier (higher per capita), estimate France's per capita between Spain/Sweden (~15-20 EUR/person/year) and UK (100 EUR/person/year), apply that estimate to France's population of 65M, and arrive at a market size around €2B. Any reasonable per capita estimate between ~20-50 EUR is acceptable.

math.setup: Per capita consumption = Online grocery sales / Population. Apply an estimated per capita to France's population of 65M.
steps: France estimate: roughly double Spain = €30/person/year (any reasonable estimate acceptable)

questions.prompt: Based on the market size alone, should our client enter the online grocery market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should say yes based on market opportunity: ~€2B top-line revenue, likely growing as online grocery penetration increases over time. Candidate should note they would also want to understand the unit economics before a final recommendation.

questions.prompt: Determine the difference in profit between the retail-only model and a retail + online model. Assume the client captures the entire ~€2B online market, 70% cannibalized from retail and 30% new sales.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that operating margins differ between channels (retail ~2.5%, online ~1.66%). They should compute the retail income lost from cannibalization and the online income gained, then net the two. The key insight is that moving online is slightly profit-negative at current scale because the online operating margin is lower than retail.

math.setup: Retail operating margin = €3 / €120 basket ≈ 2.5%. Online operating margin = €2 / €120 basket ≈ 1.66%. Cannibalized retail sales = €2B × 70% = €1.4B. New online sales = €2B.
math.answer: Net operating income impact is approximately −€2M; the move online is marginally profit-negative at current scale

questions.prompt: What are some other key areas to consider for the store to move online?
questions.guidance: No single right answer. Strong responses cover: (1) potential to close physical stores over time as online scales — but candidate should recognize risk given 85% of current sales are brick-and-mortar; (2) ways the cost position could improve as online scales (fixed cost leverage, delivery optimization); (3) risks such as unproven French online grocery demand, consumer unwillingness, competitive threats from pure-play online grocers; (4) strategic necessity — if competitors move online, the client risks further sales erosion. If candidate proposes closing stores, interviewer should push back given the 85% brick-and-mortar dependency.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some other key areas to consider for the store to move online?

categories.name: Cost & Profitability Improvement
ideas: Fixed cost leverage as online volume scales
Delivery route optimization reducing last-mile cost
Reduction in shrinkage vs physical retail

categories.name: Physical Store Strategy
ideas: Risk of closing stores given 85% of revenue is brick-and-mortar
Using existing stores as fulfillment hubs
Reducing store footprint gradually as online penetration grows

categories.name: Market & Demand Risks
ideas: Unproven French consumer appetite for online grocery
Cultural preference for fresh produce selection in-store
Low current penetration rate suggesting slower adoption

categories.name: Competitive Landscape
ideas: Pure-play online grocers (e.g., Amazon Fresh, local entrants)
Risk of inaction: competitors capturing the online channel first
Need to assess competitive response if client does not enter

categories.name: Strategic / Long-Term
ideas: Online as a defensive move to protect existing retail sales
Brand positioning and customer loyalty in digital channel
Data and personalization advantages from online platform

recommendation: At current scale, entering the online market produces a marginal −€2M net profit impact, making it economically neutral to slightly negative in the short term
However, the online grocery market is ~€2B and likely growing; not entering risks ceding the channel to competitors who could further erode the client's retail sales
risks: 70% cannibalization rate means online primarily shifts, not grows, the revenue base at this stage
Online operating margins (1.66%) are lower than retail (2.5%), so scale matters before the move becomes profitable
French consumer online grocery adoption may be slower than in comparable markets like the UK
Closing physical stores prematurely would be high risk given 85% of sales remain brick-and-mortar
risk: 70% cannibalization means online primarily shifts rather than grows the revenue base
Lower online operating margin means the business needs scale to become profitable online
French consumer adoption could lag UK benchmarks
Premature store closures risk the core business
next_steps: Conduct consumer research to validate French online grocery demand and willingness to pay
Model cost improvement scenarios as online volume scales to identify the breakeven point
Assess competitive landscape to understand urgency of market entry
